entries.title: Few-shot Prompting
entries.picture: Three finished pieces of work on the desk, not a longer briefing document.
entries.analogy: The intern read your two-page brief and still formatted it wrong. Put three completed examples in front of them and they get it in about nine seconds. Pick the three that were confusing, though — three more easy ones teach nobody anything.
entries.snapback: Target 4–6 examples at exactly the ambiguous cases where it gets things wrong. More examples of the obvious cases will not move the boundary.

entries.title: Explicit Criteria vs Vague Instructions
entries.picture: 'Use your judgement' next to a tick-list with numbers on it.
entries.analogy: Tell an intern to flag anything that 'looks off' and you will get forty things, half of them fine. Tell them to flag only where the comment claims behaviour the code does not have, and you get the four that matter.
entries.snapback: Replace abstract intent with an explicitly testable condition. 'Check accuracy' becomes 'flag only when the claimed behaviour contradicts the code'.

entries.title: Prompt Chaining
entries.picture: A relay baton going hand to hand, one runner per leg.
entries.analogy: Nobody runs the whole race carrying everything. Leg one finds the problems. Leg two writes the fixes for exactly those problems. Each runner has one job and starts from what the last one handed over.
entries.snapback: Break a complex task into sequential focused prompts, each consuming the previous step's output. More focused and more consistent than one giant prompt.

entries.title: The Interview Pattern
entries.picture: The intern asking four questions before touching the keyboard.
entries.analogy: Three drafts came back, each missing something different, because nobody in the room knew what to specify. One round of them interviewing you costs a single turn and surfaces all four unknowns at once.
entries.snapback: For an underspecified brief in a domain you do not know well, have Claude interview you first. One interview turn replaces several correction cycles.

entries.title: Validation and Retry-with-Feedback
entries.picture: Work handed back with the specific line circled in red, not a shrug.
entries.analogy: 'Do it again' teaches nothing. 'Your total says 150, the line items add to 145' fixes it on the next pass. And if the number was never on the invoice in the first place, no amount of handing it back will conjure one.
entries.snapback: Send the original input, the failed output and the specific validation error. Retry fixes format, structure and arithmetic — never genuinely absent information.

entries.title: Self-correction
entries.picture: Two totals written side by side, with a box that ticks when they disagree.
entries.analogy: You do not ask the intern 'are you sure?' — they will say yes. You make them write down the total as printed, then add the items up themselves, and put both numbers on the form. The disagreement becomes a field, not a feeling.
entries.snapback: Build the re-derivation into the output schema: stated_total, calculated_total, conflict_detected. Structural, not a conversational follow-up.

entries.title: Batches: Overview
entries.picture: A service counter: half price, back within twenty-four hours.
entries.analogy: You hand over the bag and walk away. It comes back for half what the express counter charges. Nobody at any point tells you when.
entries.snapback: The Batch API processes asynchronously at 50% of the cost, with a window of up to 24 hours.

entries.title: Batch API vs Synchronous API
entries.picture: The overnight bag versus the shirt you need pressed while you wait.
entries.analogy: Bedding, towels, the winter coat — all of that goes in the overnight bag and you save half. The shirt for the interview in forty minutes does not go in the overnight bag, no matter what it costs.
entries.snapback: Batch for non-blocking, latency-tolerant work: overnight reports, weekly audits, bulk document runs. Synchronous for anything a human or a pipeline is waiting on.

entries.title: Using custom_id
entries.picture: A name tag sewn into every shirt before it goes in the bag.
entries.analogy: Forty shirts go in. Forty come back, in whatever order the machine felt like. Without a name tag you are holding up each one asking whose this is, and you will get it wrong.
entries.snapback: Results can arrive in any order. custom_id is the join key back to the originating request — never rely on ordering.

entries.title: Handling Failures in Batches
entries.picture: Ninety-five clean shirts, five with a stain, and only five going back in.
entries.analogy: You do not rewash the whole load because five came back marked. You pull the five, work out what the stain actually was, treat it, and send back exactly those five.
entries.snapback: Identify failures by custom_id, fix the cause — chunk the long documents, say — then re-submit only the failures. Re-sending all 100 pays twice for the 95.

entries.title: SLA Planning
entries.picture: A calendar with the drop-off marked a full day before the deadline.
entries.analogy: 'It usually comes back in an hour' is a story about the average day. The counter promises twenty-four. You plan against the promise, because the one time it takes twenty-three hours is the morning you needed it.
entries.snapback: Submission deadline = downstream deadline − 24h. Plan against the worst case, never the typical observed time.

entries.title: Fixed Pipelines (Prompt Chaining)
entries.picture: A printed itinerary with every stop already listed.
entries.analogy: Same route every time. Same five stops, same order, and you can hand the sheet to anyone and get the same trip back. Perfect when the road genuinely does not change.
entries.snapback: Use a fixed sequential pipeline when the structure is predictable and every step is known in advance — reviews that always follow one template.

entries.title: Dynamic Adaptive Decomposition
entries.picture: A satnav rerouting the moment a road closes.
entries.analogy: You know roughly where you are going. You do not know that the bridge is shut until you get to the bridge. The plan for the rest of the journey is written after you find out.
entries.snapback: Generate subtasks from what earlier steps discover. Correct when the scope is unknown up front — mapping a legacy codebase before deciding what to test.

entries.title: Multi-pass Code Review
entries.picture: One pass per street, then one pass over the whole map for the one-way conflicts.
entries.analogy: Survey fourteen streets in a single sweep and you will do three of them properly and glance at the rest. Do them one at a time, then take one more run over the whole map looking only for where they contradict each other.
entries.snapback: Per-file passes for local issues, then a separate integration pass for cross-file problems. A bigger context window does not fix attention dilution.

entries.title: When to Escalate to a Human
entries.picture: A triage board with four hard criteria on it, and no box for 'seems upset'.
entries.analogy: The nurse escalates on things you can point at: the protocol does not cover this, they asked for the doctor by name, three attempts have failed, the decision is above the desk. Volume is not on the board.
entries.snapback: Escalate on structural signals — policy gap, explicit request for a human, no progress after real attempts, high-stakes ambiguity.

entries.title: Escalation Patterns
entries.picture: Someone shouting who can be helped, next to someone quietly asking for the doctor.
entries.analogy: The loud one usually has a problem you can fix in ninety seconds. Acknowledge it, offer the fix, and only move them along if they ask a second time. The quiet request for the doctor goes through immediately, first time of asking.
entries.snapback: An explicit request for a human escalates at once. Frustration alone does not — acknowledge, offer a resolution, and escalate if they reiterate.

entries.title: Structured Handoff Protocols
entries.picture: The handover sheet the next shift reads, because they never saw the patient arrive.
entries.analogy: The incoming nurse was not there for any of it. Everything they will ever know is on that one sheet: who, what is wrong, what has already been tried, what you recommend. A shrug and 'they're upset about something' is not a handover.
entries.snapback: The human has no transcript access. The summary must carry customer ID, root cause, the amount, actions already taken and a recommended action.

entries.title: Confidence Calibration and Human Oversight
entries.picture: An overall pass rate of 97%, and one ward inside it running at 60%.
entries.analogy: The hospital-wide number looks excellent, and it is hiding one ward where things go wrong four times in ten. You do not find that by staring harder at the average — you find it by checking each ward on its own.
entries.snapback: Score confidence per field, tune thresholds against labelled data, and sample the automated stream in a stratified way. Aggregate accuracy hides per-segment failure.
